summary: Explains how to decode facsimile data coming from the Rapicom 450 fax machine. It is a companion to the memo describing that machine's file format.

eli5.summary: A fax machine sends a picture in a secret code. This memo is the codebook for reading the code back into a picture.

subtitle: How to decode the compressed image data from Rapicom 450 facsimile machines.

tldr.problem: Rapicom 450 facsimile machines compress images using a complex two-dimensional run-length encoding scheme with bit-reversals and finite-state transitions. Decoding this format requires understanding the algorithm in detail.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the state machine and run-length encoding used by the Rapicom 450, including bit-reversal rules, header fields, and the block structure (sync code, header, 512 data bits, CRC checksum). It provides the decoding algorithm as a finite-state automaton and detailed parsing rules.
tldr.outcome: A program can decode Rapicom 450 fax data into standard bitmaps that can be displayed or edited using other tools.

today: RFC 798 is a historical specification for decoding facsimile data from Rapicom 450 machines, which are no longer in use. The techniques described—run-length encoding, finite-state machines, and bit-level manipulation—remain relevant to data format design and compression, but this particular RFC documents a legacy system.

sections.title: The Rapicom 450 Encoding Scheme
sections.content: RFC 798 documents the algorithm used by the Rapicom 450 facsimile machine to encode documents into a compressed bitstream. A standard 8.5-by-11-inch document contains about 2100 scan lines, each with 1726 picture elements (pels). The machine offers three quality modes: fine-detail mode encodes every line; quality mode encodes every other line (to be replicated on playback); express mode encodes every third line. Data is encoded two lines at a time using a two-dimensional run-length scheme that exploits patterns in consecutive lines.
sections.eli5: The fax machine scans your document line by line. Instead of sending each black or white square, it uses a clever code that says 'the next 50 squares are white' or 'the next 20 are black.' High quality means it scans every line, but lower quality modes skip lines to save time.

sections.title: State Machine and Run-Length Encoding
sections.content: The encoding uses a finite-state automaton with four states representing pairs of consecutive pixels (top and bottom): state 0 (W-W, both white), state 1 (W-B, top white, bottom black), state 2 (B-W), and state 3 (B-B, both black). Transitions between states are labeled with variable-length bit sequences (e.g., 101 to transition from state 1 to state 2). In states 0 and 3 (both pixels the same color), a special run-length encoding is used: a variable-sized counter (2 to 7 bits) specifies how many additional columns of that state should be emitted. The field length can grow if needed. Transitions from states 1 and 2 to different states produce fixed bit patterns. The RFC warns that the Rapicom 450 sends each field's bits in reverse order—the order must be inverted during decoding.
sections.eli5: The state machine is like a game where you're in one of four positions and each move (transition) outputs a code. When you stay in the same position many times, you use a run-length counter instead of repeating the code. But beware: the bits are sent backwards!

sections.title: Block Structure and Header Fields
sections.content: Data from the fax machine is organized into 585-bit blocks, each consisting of a 24-bit sync code (30474730 octal), a 37-bit header, 512 bits of data, and a 12-bit CRC checksum. The header contains: a 2-bit sequence number (0–3, cycling for data blocks); 5 flag bits (Run, Cofb, Rpt, Spare, Sub); a 10-bit data count (number of valid data bits to use); a 12-bit X position (current horizontal position on scan line); 3-bit black run-length field size; 3-bit white run-length field size; and a 2-bit state. Important: most header fields are sent in reversed bit order, except the sequence number and state, which are not reversed. The data count field specifies how many of the 512 data bits are valid; the remainder should be ignored. If X position exceeds 1726 (the line width) or is less than the previous position, special handling applies.
sections.eli5: Each block is like a puzzle with a wrapper. The wrapper (the header) says what scan line we're on, how many bits are real data, what state we're starting in, and how wide the run-length counters should be. Much of the wrapper is written backwards, which is confusing but part of the spec.
